questions.q: Why does provisioning speed in the cloud create a governance challenge?
options: A storage account or S3 bucket can exist in minutes, often with no procurement or governance review
Cloud providers require a governance review before any resource can be created
It doesn't — provisioning speed has no bearing on governance
Only database resources can be provisioned quickly; storage still requires approval
questions.explain: Anyone with console access and a credit card can spin up storage in minutes, with sensitive data in it shortly after — no ticket, no review, unless policy explicitly prevents it.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call treating "non-production" as a synonym for "ungoverned" a costly mistake?
options: Because real customer data regularly ends up in dev or test environments through copies, debugging, and exports
Because non-production environments never contain any data worth protecting
Because cloud providers automatically apply production-grade security to every environment regardless of labeling
Because dev and test environments are technically incapable of experiencing data breaches
questions.explain: Dev and test environments frequently end up holding real customer data via database copies, debugging sessions, or sample exports -- weak access control there is just as much a breach as the same gap in production.

questions.q: What is AWS Organizations' equivalent of an Azure management group?
options: An organizational unit (OU)
A resource group
An availability zone
A service control policy
questions.explain: Organizational units (OUs) group AWS accounts the same way Azure management groups group subscriptions — a common pattern uses OUs like Security, Production, Non-Production, and Sandbox.

questions.q: How does AWS describe the two halves of the shared responsibility model?
options: Security of the cloud (the provider's job) versus security in the cloud (the customer's job)
Security during business hours versus security after hours
Security for free-tier accounts versus security for paid accounts
Security for the United States region versus security for all other regions
questions.explain: AWS's own terminology splits responsibility into security OF the cloud (physical infrastructure, the provider's job) and security IN the cloud (data, identity, configuration — the customer's job).

questions.q: Why does assigning access to a group rather than an individual reduce governance risk?
options: Membership changes automatically grant or revoke access, with nothing for anyone to remember to update
Groups are technically incapable of being over-permissioned, unlike individuals
AWS and Azure both forbid assigning roles directly to individual users
Group-based access never needs to be reviewed or audited
questions.explain: When a role or policy is attached to a group, a new hire joining or someone leaving the team automatically grants or revokes their access -- no separate step to remember, unlike per-individual assignments.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say identity is the governance layer everything else depends on?
options: You can't meaningfully restrict access, enforce policy, or produce useful audit logs for a principal the system can't reliably identify
Because identity is the only layer that cloud providers actually bill for
Because policy and monitoring are optional once identity is configured correctly
Because data classification automatically happens once identity is set up
questions.explain: Access restrictions, policy enforcement, and audit logging all require a trustworthy way to know who's asking — without reliable identity, every downstream governance control inherits that weakness.

questions.q: What question does Azure RBAC answer, as distinct from Microsoft Entra ID?
options: What is a given identity allowed to do to a specific resource, resource group, subscription, or management group
Who is allowed to sign into the Azure portal at all
Which users exist in the directory and what groups they belong to
How billing is split across subscriptions
questions.explain: Azure RBAC is resource-scoped authorization, answering what an identity can do to a specific resource — a narrower question than Entra ID's directory-level "who can manage the tenant itself."

questions.q: Where do you find built-in directory roles in the Microsoft Entra admin center?
options: Identity → Roles & admins → Roles & admins
Billing → Cost Management → Roles
Settings → Subscriptions → Access control (IAM)
Home → Resource groups → Roles
questions.explain: Every built-in directory role lives on the Roles and administrators page, reached via Identity → Roles & admins → Roles & admins in the Entra admin center.

questions.q: Why does Block Public Access exist as a separate layer from bucket policies at all?
options: It acts as an override safety switch that refuses to honor public grants from a policy or ACL, without needing to edit that policy itself
It replaces bucket policies entirely once enabled
It is required before any bucket policy can be attached to a bucket
It only affects objects uploaded before 2023
questions.explain: Block Public Access doesn't change the policy or ACL — it sits on top and refuses to honor the public parts of whatever access rules already exist.

questions.q: Why does Microsoft recommend assigning ACL entries to Microsoft Entra groups instead of individual users?
options: A group's membership only needs updating once, rather than hunting down every individual ACL entry when someone changes roles
ACLs technically cannot be assigned to individual user accounts
Groups get automatic Execute permission on all parent folders
It removes the need for Azure RBAC entirely
questions.explain: Individual-user ACL entries become a cleanup burden as people change teams; group-based ACLs only need the group membership changed in one place.

questions.q: In Microsoft Purview, what does registering a data source actually do?
options: Tells Purview the source exists and which collection it belongs to — it does not extract any metadata yet
Immediately scans the entire source and classifies every column
Grants every Purview user read access to the underlying data
Deletes the source from its original storage account
questions.explain: Registration is a lightweight step that just makes Purview aware of the source and its collection. Metadata extraction happens in a separate scan.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what changed between Version 3 and Version 7 of the same table?
options: Two columns gained 'Sensitive Data Element' comments flagging EMAIL and USA_SSN, from an automated classification job
The table was renamed
The S3 location changed to a different bucket
The number of columns doubled
questions.explain: The schema structure stayed the same (still 4 string columns), but comments were added identifying two columns as containing sensitive data — a common pattern after an automated PII detection pass.

questions.q: How long does CloudTrail's Event history retain management events by default?
options: The last 90 days, for the current AWS Region
Indefinitely, with no retention limit
7 days
Only the current calendar day
questions.explain: Event history is a rolling 90-day window by default — the same default retention period as the Azure Activity Log.

questions.q: What's the difference between an assignment that 'floats' on a built-in definition's version versus one that's 'pinned'?
options: A floating assignment automatically picks up new minor/patch versions as Microsoft updates the definition; a pinned one stays on an exact version
Pinned assignments are always deleted after 90 days
Floating assignments only work with custom definitions, never built-in ones
There is no functional difference — both terms mean the same thing
questions.explain: Floating is the default and picks up definition updates automatically. Pinning locks to an exact version, which matters more for Deny or auto-remediation policies.

questions.q: What does the 'Origin' field on an AWS KMS key's Cryptographic configuration tab indicate?
options: Where the key material came from — AWS KMS-generated, imported, or backed by AWS CloudHSM
Which AWS Region the key was created in
The IAM user who created the key
Whether the key is symmetric or asymmetric
questions.explain: Origin specifically describes the source of the key material (AWS KMS, imported/external, or CloudHSM-backed), distinct from Key Type, Key Spec, and Key Usage.

questions.q: What is a service control policy (SCP), fundamentally?
options: A permission ceiling that sets the maximum available permissions for IAM users and roles in covered accounts — it never grants anything by itself
An IAM policy that directly grants permissions to users
A billing policy that controls spending limits
A resource tag used for cost allocation
questions.explain: An SCP is a ceiling, not a grant — it can only narrow what IAM policies in the account are allowed to permit, never add permissions on its own.

questions.q: Once an AWS S3 source is scanned, how do its assets appear in the Purview Unified Catalog, per this lesson?
options: Exactly like any Azure asset — filterable by asset type, with the same classification facets, in the same search results
In a completely separate catalog that cannot be searched together with Azure assets
Only as raw file names with no classification information
They do not appear in the catalog at all, only in a separate report
questions.explain: A steward can search the catalog and get Azure and AWS results in the same list, without needing to know which cloud the data physically lives on.

questions.q: Is Briarcliff Outdoor Gear, the company in this case study, a real business?
options: No — it's explicitly described as a fictional, illustrative composite scenario
Yes — it is a real, named outdoor retailer
Yes — it is a real company whose name was changed for privacy
The lesson does not say whether it is real or fictional
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly labels Briarcliff Outdoor Gear as fictional and illustrative, consistent with this catalog's policy against presenting invented scenarios as real.

questions.q: What is 'policy drift,' as defined in this lesson?
options: When the same governance rule is enforced with different strictness on one cloud than the other, because two parallel rule sets aren't being actively compared
When a cloud provider changes its pricing without notice
When a user's password expires on one cloud but not another
When a company migrates entirely from one cloud to another
questions.explain: Policy drift happens when maintaining two parallel rule sets lets the second one quietly fall behind the first — not through a deliberate decision, but through neglect.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what column does the lab say most real-world control maps skip, and why does it matter?
options: An 'owner' column naming who is responsible for keeping both sides of each row in sync — without it, there's no one accountable for catching drift
A column listing the exact dollar cost of each cloud service
A column listing the company's stock ticker symbol
A column counting the total number of employees at the company
questions.explain: An honestly 'unassigned' owner is more useful than a map that looks complete but isn't backed by anyone's actual responsibility.
